title: Asma Came by Night, as She Often Does
intro: Al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi includes this poem by Amr ibn al-Ahtam in his Mufaddaliyyat. Asma visits him in a dream, then gives way to a conversation with Umm Haytham about what a household can afford to give. Amr answers with the story of a traveller who finds his camp on a winter night. The meal and bedding he provides lead to a distinction between cramped quarters and a narrow welcome.

translation: Asma came by night, as she often does,
and left, though even her phantom stirs longing.
1.sharh: The nightly visitor can reach him across a separation that her waking self cannot cross. The familiar visit leaves him missing her all over again.

translation: She left with the longing of a grieving man whose heart
is a wing with both bones failing, still beating.
2.sharh: The flutter belongs equally to a heart and to an injured wing. The bird can still beat it, although it has lost the strength to take flight.

translation: Asma takes the long distance lightly.
A man distraught with love yearns and aches for her.
3.sharh: The distance is the same for both lovers and costs them quite different things. Amr lets us see himself from outside as the man still looking her way.

translation: Leave me be, Umm Haytham. Stinginess
is a practised thief of all that is good in men.
4.sharh: Money kept back has another cost. The intensive form of “thief” makes stinginess an old hand at stripping a person of his better qualities.

translation: Let me be, and come round to what I wish.
I am anxious for the honour that has grown so high.
5.sharh: His plea turns on what each of them is trying to protect. The family standing built up over time is something a single inhospitable act could damage.

translation: I am generous and have mouths to feed. I feel the weight
of losses that descend on us and claims I must meet.
6.sharh: He speaks as someone who knows the household accounts. A sudden loss and an obligation to another person both make real demands on his means.

translation: Many a man barked for shelter after all fell quiet. I called him in
as a winter star was about to set.
7.sharh: A lost traveller would bark in the hope of rousing camp dogs and finding the tents by their answer. Amr answers the signal by offering a place in his camp.

translation: He was battling the bitter onset of the night.
Winds twisted his cloak about him, and lightning
8.sharh: The night has a projecting front like the bridge of a nose, something the man has to meet head on. The lightning at the end flashes on into the next verse.

translation: flashed in the heart of a rain-bearing cloud,
its low fringe streaming down in torrents.
9.sharh: The lightning reveals the density of the cloud. What hangs beneath it looks like a fringe, except that the strands reaching towards the traveller are falling water.

translation: I took him in. I spoke no harsh word
and never pleaded lack of room to turn him away.
10.sharh: A stranger has little means of questioning a host who says there is no room. Amr makes what he refrained from saying the first act of hospitality.

translation: I said, “Welcome. There’s room here, and easy ground.
Your morning drink is assured, and you have a friend.”
11.sharh: The familiar words of welcome offer kin, level ground and ample space. Promising a morning drink already gives the newcomer leave to stay the night.

translation: I went to the sleeping herd. They shielded themselves,
great high-humped beauties like towers,
12.sharh: The crouching shapes are substantial enough to suggest fortresses. The sentence leaves the herd sheltering behind something and waits a whole line to show us what it is.

translation: behind a pale cow, an early calver, who looked,
crossing in front of the pregnant cows, like a prize stallion.
13.sharh: The cow is outstanding among valuable breeding animals. Her early calving and the size that could make her pass for a prized male bring home the cost of the meal.

translation: A blow to the shank, or a deep thrust that pours freely
from an opening in front of the shoulders.
14.sharh: The action has narrowed from the silhouette of the herd to an animal’s shank and the hollow before its shoulders. Hospitality requires an animal of his own to die.

translation: Two butchers climbed up over her,
whisking away the hide as her breath came in gasps.
15.sharh: The two men’s hands work so fast the hide seems to fly. Against that speed Amr sets the animal’s intermittent final breaths.

translation: Her udder and hump were drawn towards us,
and a bright, well-bred calf struggling to its feet.
16.sharh: After the cuts brought over for the meal comes an unexpected movement. The pale calf is alive and trying to stand.

translation: A calf cut from the womb. The man who cleared its covering away
with his blade was a companion gentle in friendship.
17.sharh: The blade that opened the dam also frees the calf from its membrane. The handling of this vulnerable animal earns the helper a word about his gentleness.

translation: Late that night there was for us and our guest
rich roast meat running with fat, and an evening drink.
18.sharh: The host includes his own people at the meal. The evening milk and the promised drink at dawn make the stay encompass more than a single helping of meat.

translation: Between him and the bitter east wind that night
lay a coverlet and a fine, smooth cloak.
19.sharh: The wind once twisted his cloak around him. The blanket and fine covering now keep it out. Al-Asma'i understood the smooth covering as the skin on cooling milk, another kindness a host could offer.

translation: Every generous man keeps blame away by feeding guests.
Goodness has a well-trodden path among the decent.
20.sharh: The story of one household becomes a shared practice. The figure of a path has a particular force after the traveller who needed help finding his way.

translation: By your life, a country never grew too cramped for its people.
It is men’s dispositions that grow cramped.
21.sharh: The cramped lodging he refused to plead now explains the maxim. Amr uses the same verb for land and for character, making a refusal of shelter a decision a person takes.

translation: Roots from Zurara raised me to the heights,
with roots from Fadaki and al-Ashadd.
22.sharh: The names put a genealogy behind the deed just described. The roots reach down, and what they have inherited carries the speaker upwards.

translation: Such virtues set a young man on a lofty stock,
though some who beget children count for little.
23.sharh: He names the worth that can pass from parent to child. Before laying claim to such ancestry he has let the listener watch him put it into practice.

1.1.2.head: طَرَقَ
1.1.2.meaning: Visited after dark, often of a beloved appearing in a dream.

1.2.4.head: الخَيال
1.2.4.meaning: The apparition of an absent person in sleep.

2.2.2.meaning: Grew weak or lost its firmness.

2.2.5.head: خَفوق
2.2.5.meaning: Fluttering repeatedly, of a wing or a heart.

3.1.5-6.meaning: “The destination grew distant”, of a journey that separates lovers.

3.2.3.head: والِه
3.2.3.meaning: Distraught or bewildered with love or grief.

4.1.5-6.head: أُمّ هَيثَم
4.1.5-6.meaning: Umm Haytham, the woman whom Amr addresses about his generosity.

4.2.4.head: سَروق
4.2.4.meaning: An inveterate thief, an intensive form.

5.1.2-4.head: حُطّي في هَواي
5.1.2-4.meaning: “Set down where my desire rests”, join me in the course I choose.

5.2.2.head: الحَسَب
5.2.2.meaning: A family’s accumulated claim to honour.

6.2.3.head: رُزء
6.2.3.meaning: A loss, here a loss borne by the household.

7.1.1.head: مُستَنبِح
7.1.1.meaning: A night traveller who imitates a bark to locate camp dogs.

7.2.4-5.head: نَجم الشِّتاء
7.2.4-5.meaning: “The winter star”, the Pleiades in the commentary.

8.1.2.head: عِرنين
8.1.2.meaning: The bridge of a nose, here the advancing front of night.

9.2.2.head: هَيدَب
9.2.2.meaning: A hanging fringe of cloud or a trailing curtain of rain.

11.2.2.head: صَبوح
11.2.2.meaning: A drink taken in the morning, often milk.

12.1.3-4.head: البَرك الهَواجِد
12.1.3-4.meaning: “The sleeping herd”, camels resting on their folded legs.

12.2.1-2.head: مَقاحيد كوم
12.2.1-2.meaning: Fine camels with large, high humps.

12.2.3.head: المَجادِل
12.2.3.meaning: High, solidly built towers or strongholds.

13.1.2-3.head: مِرباع النِّتاج
13.1.2-3.meaning: A she-camel that habitually calves early in the season.

13.2.4.head: العِشار
13.2.4.meaning: She-camels ten months gone in calf.

14.1.4-5.head: نَجلاء ثَرَّة
14.1.4-5.meaning: A wide wound from which blood flows abundantly.

15.1.4.head: أَوفَدَ
15.1.4.meaning: Rose over the animal, also understood as making haste.

16.2.1.head: أَزهَر
16.2.1.meaning: Bright or pale in colour, here the camel calf.

17.1.1.head: بَقير
17.1.1.meaning: A young animal taken from its mother by opening the womb.

18.1.5.head: مَوهِن
18.1.5.meaning: A time well into the night.

18.2.4.head: غَبوق
18.2.4.meaning: An evening draught, the counterpart of the morning drink.

20.1.5.head: القِرى
20.1.5.meaning: The food and entertainment furnished to a guest.

22.1.4.head: زُرارَة
22.1.4.meaning: Zurara ibn Udas, a Tamimi chief in the poet’s maternal ancestry.

22.2.2.head: فَدَكِيّ
22.2.2.meaning: Fadaki, father of Mayya, the poet’s mother.

22.2.3.head: الأَشَدّ
22.2.3.meaning: Al-Ashadd, the byname of Sinan ibn Khalid ibn Minqar, one of the poet’s forebears.

23.1.5.head: أَرومَة
23.1.5.meaning: The rootstock from which a lineage branches.
